I've been farming this land for 40 years, and I know every inch of my 2 mu plot in Quzhou. At 60, I don't chase fancy new tricks—I stick with what works. The wheat-maize rotation has fed my family for decades, and that's not changing.

It's the start of the season now, so I'll plant winter wheat first on the full 2 mu. I'll use improved wheat seed—hybrids cost more and I don't need the risk on my small plot. Before planting, I'll run the rotary tiller to break up the stubble from last year's maize and get a fine seedbed. For fertilizer, I'll put down about 16 kg of nitrogen per mu, 6 kg of phosphorus, and 4 kg of potassium at sowing and top-dress in spring. I'll irrigate three times: once before winter to help the seedlings establish, once at jointing when the wheat starts shooting up, and once at grain filling to plump the kernels. One pesticide spray should handle any aphids or rust that show up. I expect about 500 kg per mu from the wheat.

After wheat harvest in early June, I'll immediately till and plant summer maize—again on the full 2 mu, since there's no time to waste on the North China Plain. I'll use hybrid maize seed; the improved varieties just don't yield enough anymore. I'll apply about 17 kg nitrogen per mu, 5 kg phosphorus, and 4 kg potassium. Maize needs water at jointing and filling, so two irrigations from my well should be enough if the rains cooperate. Two pesticide applications—one early for borers, one later if leaf spot shows up. With good weather, I should get around 550 kg per mu.

This schedule keeps my family of three fed with grain to spare, and I don't take risks I can't afford.
